_comment: Five standalone films, cut from the same four screen recordings as the 90-second explainer but with their own narration. Every in/out point below was read off frame strips of the source, not guessed - see README. Scene LENGTH is never set here: each scene runs exactly as long as its narration, so re-writing a line re-times the picture automatically.

scenes.vo: Part one. Setting up your profile. You do this once, and then you are done with it.

Every job application asks you for the same things. Your name, your phone number, your address, your résumé, a signature at the bottom. Even your gender, which this app only ever asks so it can answer that question when a form insists on it. Fill it in here one time, and it is carried into every form you meet after that.
Open the menu, and tap Account Settings.
scenes.head: Menu, then Account Settings
scenes.sub: Everything about you lives here

scenes.vo: Your photo, name, email, phone, address, date of birth.
scenes.head: Your details
scenes.sub: Typed once, kept for every form

scenes.vo: Then attach your résumé, straight from your phone.
scenes.head: Attach your résumé
scenes.sub: PDF or Word, straight from your phone

scenes.vo: That is the file it attaches for you later.
scenes.head: Uploaded

scenes.vo: Save, and the setup is done.
scenes.head: Saved

scenes.vo: Next, we turn that into a résumé built for the country you are applying to.
Part two. Building your résumé, and formatting it for wherever you are applying.

card.sub: And formatted for where you apply

scenes.vo: Here is the part nobody tells you. Before a person ever reads your résumé, software reads it first, and it is trying to pull out your name, your dates, your job titles and your skills. The handsome two column template, with the icons and the little skill bars, is exactly where that goes wrong. So the app rates every one of its formats on how cleanly it reads to that software. The five star ones are built to be understood by the machine first, and admired by the human second.
scenes.note: Claim check: the five-star rating is the app's own ATS rating, shown on the template picker and defined in server/utils/resumeTemplates.js. No percentile or success-rate claim is made anywhere in this film.

scenes.vo: What comes back is structured, not just tidied up.
scenes.head: Structured, not just tidied
scenes.sub: Summary · experience · skills

scenes.vo: And a résumé is not the same document everywhere in the world. A German CV is expected to carry a photo. A US résumé must not have one. India, the United Kingdom, Singapore, the European Union — each has its own shape, and getting it wrong is the sort of thing that quietly costs you an interview, and you never find out why. Choose your region here, and the whole document is rebuilt to fit it.
Swipe the formats for your region. Each one carries that star rating.

scenes.vo: Part three. Finding a job, and handing the homework over.

Every application you take seriously starts with the same unpaid hour. Reading the posting properly. Working out what the company actually does. Digging out the salary, the skills they want, and who you should be writing to. Save the job here instead, and that whole list moves across to the app. You spend your time applying, not researching.

scenes.vo: Part four. The cover letter.

card.sub: Written for that job, at that company

scenes.vo: A generic cover letter is worse than sending none at all, because everybody can spot the template. A good one names what the company actually does, and connects it to what you have actually done. That is an hour of work for every single application, which is why almost nobody writes one every time. Here, it is one tap.
scenes.note: The 'one tap' claim is what the recording shows: the AI Cover Letter card is a single button. No wall-clock time is claimed for generation.

scenes.vo: One thing left. Did you know the app can fill in the employer's form for you, and apply? That is the last one.
Part five. The one that saves the most time — filling in the employer's own application form.

This is where applications quietly die. You have the résumé, you have the letter, and now there is a thirty field form on a portal you have never seen before, asking you for everything you have already written down twice. Auto Fill reads that form and completes it from your profile. On their site, not ours.
From the job, tap Apply on Portal.
